title: Lamed
hook: the tallest letter; lamad means learn

segments.voice: Yesterday, kaf, the palm: the sole of the dove's foot, the hand stretched to the poor. Your line was open palm. What did you hand over slowly? Today, a letter that reaches up. Day one thousand three hundred forty.

The room is loud. Not a quiet library hush, the other kind. Long tables, big books open, and at the tables, pairs of people leaning toward each other, arguing. One reads a line aloud. The other says, wait, that can't be right, look at this word. Someone laughs. Someone thumps the page. This is a beit midrash, a study hall, and the noise is the point: in this kind of room, learning is done out loud, in pairs, with someone who will push back. Over the door of a room like this, you could hang a single letter. It would stick up above all the others.
screen: `A LOUD ROOM.` → `TWO PEOPLE, ONE BOOK.` → `THE STUDY HALL.`

segments.voice: Lamed. Look at it first. The letters around it sit between two invisible lines, top and bottom. Lamed doesn't stay put. Its neck rises above the top line, and teachers of the alef-bet call it the tallest letter. A letter reaching for something higher. Now listen to it. Lamed opens the verb for learning. Lamad: he learned. Limed: he taught. A student is a talmid. A teacher is a melamed. And the great collection of the rabbis' discussions is the Talmud. Listen for the same three letters, l, m, d, in each one: the student, the teacher and the book. Then hear how the Torah uses it. When Moses gathers the people to repeat the commandments, in the King James he says: "Hear, O Israel, the statutes and judgments which I speak in your ears this day, that ye may learn them, and keep, and do them." Learn, then keep, then do. Learning comes first in the line, and doing comes out of it. Finally, a warning about how learning goes wrong. In Pirkei Avot, the sayings of the sages, Hillel teaches that someone too shy to ask cannot learn, and someone too impatient cannot teach. Both sides of lamed need something. The student has to be willing to look foolish for a moment. The teacher has to be willing to explain it again. Some days, that's the whole lesson. The tall letter isn't tall because it knows everything. It's reaching. Every real question you ask is a little lamed, sticking up above the line.
screen: `A NECK ABOVE THE LINE.` · `LAMAD, TALMID, MELAMED, TALMUD.` · `LEARN, KEEP, DO.` · `THE SHY CANNOT LEARN.` · then, large: `ASK THE QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one thing to learn. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something you've been pretending to understand. A word you nod along to. How something works at your job. A prayer you've heard but never looked up. Something about a person close to you that you've never asked. Name it plainly to yourself: I don't know this yet. Notice if there's a little embarrassment, and let it be there. Then picture asking the question out loud, the way they do in the study hall. If you pray, you can ask for understanding. The bell holds the time.
Lamed. The tall letter, rising above the line, carrying the root of learning: lamad, talmid, Talmud. Today's word.
Your line: lamed learns. Today, ask the question you named, out loud, to someone who might know. Day one thousand three hundred forty.

howItsDone: In a beit midrash, a study hall, students may learn in pairs called chavruta, reading texts aloud and arguing over them; Torah study, talmud torah, is counted in Jewish tradition as a commandment in its own right.

fork.setup: you don't understand the line your study partner just read. everyone else seems to. what does Hillel's teaching in Pirkei Avot point you toward?
options: stay quiet so you don't look foolish.
ask, because the shy cannot learn.

fork.reveal: Hillel teaches that the one too shy to ask cannot learn, and the one too impatient cannot teach.

original.note: Hebrew: he learned. The letter lamed (ל) begins it; the same letters, l-m-d, run through talmid, student, and Talmud.

trapdoor: what you thought: lamed is just the l sound.
what it means: the tall letter that carries the root of learning.
what a scholar hears: l-m-d runs through lamad and limed, learn and teach, talmid and melamed, and the Talmud itself; Deuteronomy 5:1 puts learning before keeping and doing.
